articles.title: Watch: Six-year-old girl from China sets new Rubik's Cube world record
articles.summary: Lian Yunzhi broke the women's world record twice in three days at World Cube Association competitions.
articles.full_text:
Watch: Six-year-old girl from China sets new Rubik's Cube world record
Watch: Six-year-old girl from China sets new Rubik's Cube world record 
Close 
A young girl has broken the women's world record for the 3x3x3 Rubik's Cube twice in three days at the World Cube Association. 
At age six, Lian Yunzhi has become the only female cuber in the world to have an average time under 4.5 seconds. She first broke the record with an average of 4.52 seconds and then 4.27 seconds at competitions in Wuhan and Guangzhou, China. 
The young competitor from Sichuan Province has mastered more than 1,300 Rubik's Cube solving algorithms after vigorous training that involved spending two to three hours a day on the cube over the past year.

articles.title: Yu, 13, wins record-breaking first major gold medal
articles.summary: China’s Yu Zidi, 13, wins a record‑breaking 200m women’s butterfly gold at the Asian Games in Tokyo.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Yu won gold by over three seconds in Tokyo 
- Published 20 September 2026 
Chinese schoolgirl Yu Zidi lit up the opening day of the Asian Games with a record‑breaking 200m butterfly gold medal secured by a performance she described as "only so‑so". 
The 13‑year‑old claimed her first major gold in two minutes 05.08 seconds, an Asian Games record that took almost half a second off compatriot Zhang Yufei's mark from three years ago. 
Yu, who is strongly tipped to make an impact at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, won by over three seconds in Tokyo from her team-mate Chang Mohan. 
"It was only so-so," a smiling Yu said after receiving her medal, adding that her butterfly technique "is still slightly lacking". 
"I hope I can swim even faster. I improved my time by 0.9 seconds here, and I believe I will perform better next time," she continued. 
Yu, who will take part in two more individual events at the Asian Games, became the youngest ever swimmer to win a medal at the World Championships when she took bronze as a 12-year-old as part of China's 4x200m freestyle relay team last year.

articles.title: Sri Lanka court convicts 15 men over deadly Easter Sunday bombings
articles.summary: Three churches and three luxury hotels were targeted in the 2019 attacks which killed 270.
articles.full_text:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Dozens of police and commandos were deployed to the courtroom before the verdicts were announced By Ishara Danasekara ,  BBC Sinhala   and   Kumudu Jayawardana ,  BBC Sinhala 
- Published 22 September 2026 
Sri Lanka's High Court has given long jail sentences to 15 men charged with plotting the 2019 Easter Sunday bomb attacks that killed 270 people and injured more than 500. 
Those found guilty include Naufer Moulavi, who prosecutors said masterminded the suicide bombings. Nine other men were acquitted. 
The co-ordinated blasts at three churches and three luxury hotels were the deadliest in Sri Lanka since the end of its civil war in 2009. Forty-five foreigners were among the dead. 
All the bombers who carried out the attacks died in the blasts. Investigators have previously blamed the bombings on Islamist extremists, and the 25 men indicted were from Sri Lanka's Muslim minority. One died in custody. 
The 15 defendants on Tuesday were each given prison terms ranging from 200 to 260 years. 
The court in the capital Colombo also ordered the confiscation of their all movable and immovable assets. 
The accused, who had been charged with more than 23,000 offences, were handcuffed in pairs and brought to the court in two prison buses. 
Most of those killed were Sri Lankans, many of whom were children. 
They included celebrity chef Shantha Mayadunne and her daughter, an entire young family of five, at least eight members of staff from the hotels targeted and five members of the same family from the western Sri Lankan city of Negombo. 
The foreigners who died included 11 Indians, eight Britons and five Americans . 
Among the dead there were also citizens of Australia, Bangladesh, China, Denmark, Japan, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and Turkey. 
Three of Danish billionaire Anders Holch Povlsen's children died in the attack on the Shangri-La hotel, while the family had been holidaying there. 
'Intelligence lapse' 
In the wake of the attacks, Sri Lankan authorities pointed to a "major intelligence lapse". Its parliament heard that a tip-off from India about the attacks was not properly shared with the authorities. 
In 2023, the Supreme Court ordered former president Maithripala Sirisena to pay millions in compensation to the victims of the bombings, after finding him responsible for national security failures that led to the attacks. 
Last month, two former senior officials were sentenced to death for criminal negligence that led to the bombings. Death sentences are usually commuted to life in prison in Sri Lanka due to a decades-old moratorium on executions. 
For years, Sri Lankans have held regular demonstrations demanding justice for the victims of the Easter attacks. 
The verdict comes as a separate investigation into former intelligence chief Suresh Sallay is under way. Sallay is accused of orchestrating the bombings with Islamist extremists. 
The allegations echo those aired in a 2023 documentary by British broadcaster Channel 4, which heard whistleblower testimony claiming the attacks were allowed to happen to boost the popularity of the Rajapaksa family, which long dominated Sri Lankan politics. 
Sallay, who was arrested in February, denies the allegations. Former president Gotabaya Rajapaksa, who was elected months after the 2019 attacks, with a campaign of tackling Islamist extremism has also denied the allegations. 
Rajapaksa, who has been banned from leaving the country, has asked the court to prevent his potential arrest in connection with the ongoing investigations.

articles.title: Nvidia boss rejects AI extinction fears as 'doomsday narratives'
articles.summary: Jensen Huang's comments come after warnings from AI researchers that the technology could lead to human extinction.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images By Osmond Chia Business reporter 
- Published 21 September 2026 
Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has described warnings that AI could lead to humanity's extinction by the next decade as "doomsday narratives". 
"2030 is not going to be the end of the world. There is 0% chance that's going to be the end of the world", Huang said in an interview with CBS News, the BBC's US partner. 
Huang added: "Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible." 
Warnings from researchers in recent weeks about potential risks posed by the technology escalated the debate about AI safety, with some industry executives calling for a slowdown in developing models. 
His remarks follow claims posted on social media by former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon that AI developers believe the technology "could kill us all by the end of the decade". 
Coxon's concerns sparked debate about the technology's risks, including calls by top executives like Anthropic boss Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman urging for AI's development to slow down. 
Huang said that such predictions are "not grounded in science", adding that it is in Nvidia's best interest to ensure the industry builds its products responsibly. 
"Our company's success is directly connected to the safe deployment of products and services," he said. "If we don't continue to do that, our value would be diminished." 
Huang suggested AI firms talking about a "slow down" could be seeking liability protections for harms their products may cause. 
"Go and read between the lines," he said. "They're actually not asking for more laws. They're asking to be relieved of the laws we do have, and I think that that's a problem." 
Huang's comments echo those from multiple people contacted by the BBC who have worked for companies including OpenAI, Meta, and DeepMind. 
In text exchanges and conversations, they said were sceptical of the idea that unchecked AI development would lead to tools that could kill people en masse. 
- 
Not all AI workers think the tech could kill everyone 
- Published 3 days ago 
- 
OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms 
- Published 6 days ago 
- 
Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they? 
- Published 5 days ago 
Nvidia is a key player in the industry, developing cutting edge computer chips that are crucial for making AI models. 
The firm's most powerful chips face restrictions in China due to measures imposed by both Washington and Beijing. 
US export controls aim to slow China's military and AI progress, while Chinese regulations are designed to encourage reliance on domestically produced technology. 
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng held talks in New York on Sunday as they try to strike deals on AI, tariffs and critical minerals. 
After the meeting, Bessent told reporters that the two sides had discussed setting up a new AI safety notification mechanism. 
It came as President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping are due to hold a summit in Washington later this week. 
Last week, Huang appeared at a UK summit hosted by King Charles , who warned tech leaders of the "existential dangers" of AI. 
"The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world," the King told the group. 
In the US, President Donald Trump has downplayed concerns about AI's risks . 
Trump made a surprise phone call to Huang while the Nvidia boss was speaking on stage at a tech conference in Los Angeles on 14 September. 
During the call, Trump criticised calls to slow the pace of AI development and dismissed fears as a "hoax".

articles.title: Why a new Pakistan-China border pact has irked India
articles.summary: A China-Pakistan border pact challenges India's territorial claims and deepens strategic concerns over disputed Kashmir.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Future Publishing via Getty Images Image caption, 
Chinese soldiers hold a field exercise in the snow near the Kunjerab Pass bordering Pakistan By Soutik Biswas 
India correspondent 
- Published 21 September 2026 
For decades, India has refused to recognise a Pakistan-China boundary in a disputed part of the Himalayas that Delhi claims as its own. 
But last week, Pakistan and China formalised a boundary in a remote part of the mountainous region, drawing a sharp response from Delhi. 
The two countries signed the Pakistan-China Boundary Joint Commission, an agreement which Pakistan described as a "significant milestone" that would deepen cooperation on border management, trade and connectivity between India's regional rivals. 
Delhi rejected the move as having no legal basis, saying it did not recognise any Pakistan-China boundary located in territory it claims as Indian. 
The announcement comes at a particularly sensitive moment. 
India and China are seeking to stabilise their relationship after years of military tensions along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the disputed line separating their forces along much of their Himalayan frontier. At the same time, Beijing and Islamabad are deepening cooperation along a neighbouring stretch of the frontier that India also claims. 
"There is no boundary between Pakistan and China. We reject the so-called Joint Commission, which is without any legal basis," Indian foreign ministry spokesman Randhir Jaiswal said. 
Image source, Corbis via Getty Images Image caption, 
The commission concerns the Pakistan-China frontier, including the Shaksgam Valley 
The commission concerns the Pakistan-China frontier, including the Shaksgam Valley, a roughly 5,180 sq km tract that Pakistan ceded to China in 1963 but which India claims as part of its territory in Ladakh. 
India says the territory was part of the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir and was illegally occupied by Pakistan before being ceded to China. The Indian government has never recognised the agreement and considers it illegal and invalid. 
This history explains the particular sensitivity of Wednesday's announcement. 
"Pakistan has no locus standi to enter into arrangements concerning Indian territory under its illegal and forcible occupation," the Indian foreign ministry said. 
Pakistan says Jammu and Kashmir remains a disputed territory, and argues that India therefore has no standing to challenge its 1963 boundary agreement with China. It regards the agreement as valid. 
Jabin T Jacob, professor at the Department of International Relations and Governance Studies at Delhi's Shiv Nadar University, said the new development represented the revival of an old mechanism rather than an entirely new arrangement. 
"A joint boundary commission is provided for in the 1963 Sino-Pak Agreement, the only issue at hand is the timing of its operationalisation," he told the BBC. 
He said there could be several reasons for the timing, including China's broader effort to demarcate its boundaries and a desire to institutionalise exchanges and movement along a frontier at a time when Pakistan's other borders have experienced conflict and instability. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
An Indian army convoy driving towards Leh on a highway bordering China 
Jacob said India should be "worried" by the development. More importantly, he said, the move appeared to disregard a provision in the 1963 treaty itself. 
Article 6 of the agreement provided for its renegotiation once the Kashmir dispute was settled with whichever country ultimately controlled the territory, Jacob said. 
For India, Jacob said, the problem is compounded by the international information environment. 
"China's relative dominance of the international media and information landscape - [with] CGTN, CRI, presence on social media - relative to India allows it to put forward its narrative and maps globally while India is limited to fulminations that other world capitals are likely to ignore," he said. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Indian Army vehicles drive on a road near a mountain pass in India's Ladakh region 
That concern is distinct from the practical management of the frontier itself. Pakistan and China already have extensive infrastructure and connectivity links across the region, including the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) and the Karakoram Highway. 
Husain Haqqani, former Pakistani ambassador to the US and now a senior fellow at Anwar Gargash Diplomatic Academy and Hudson Institute, said the new commission was both practical and political. 
"It is a combination of both," Haqqani told the BBC. "It is a mechanism to enhance border and boundary cooperation, prevent illegal crossings and protect the strategic infrastructure tied to CPEC." 
He said it also served as a signal to India that Beijing continued to view Kashmir through the Pakistani prism. 
"China has never accepted India's position on Kashmir and China views Gilgit-Baltistan from the Pakistani, not Indian prism," Haqqani said, referring to the region in Pakistan-administered Kashmir that borders China and which India claims as part of its territory. 
Haqqani said Islamabad's position had evolved in response to developments in Indian-administered Kashmir. 
"Pakistan still maintains that the final status of Jammu and Kashmir is yet to be decided," he said. "But since India has made internal changes - for example, the abrogation of Article 370 - in its part of Kashmir, Pakistan sees no issue with simply institutionalising what has been de facto with China since 1963." 
Image source, Anadolu Agency/Getty Images Image caption, 
The Gwadar port, west of Karachi, is a key part of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor 
For Beijing, the arrangement also fits into a broader pattern of using its relationships with neighbouring states to manage and signal its position towards India. 
Haqqani said reassurance to Pakistan on Kashmir was of both strategic and geopolitical value to Beijing. 
"On the strategic front it further deepens ties with Pakistan and on the geo-strategic front it reinforces for India its fear of a two-front threat from China and Pakistan, which pleases Pakistan and benefits China." 
The timing of the statement, say experts, is also significant. 
"China always plans its decisions months, if not years, in advance so the decision to operationalise a joint boundary commission must have been made some time back," says Haqqani. 
"The release of this information was timed for after President Xi Jinping's recent Brics summit trip to send Pakistan a message of reassurance in the strategic partnership, and India a reminder that multilateral engagement does not translate into any change in China's vision for South Asia." 
But Jacob cautioned against interpreting every aspect of the development as a direct military move against India. 
"There aren't any immediate or apparent implications for the LAC as of now," he said. 
That suggests that the significance of last week's announcement may lie less in an immediate change to the disputed Himalayan frontier than in the gradual institutionalisation of arrangements that India has consistently rejected. 
India's position, Jaiswal said, remained "clear and consistent": any attempt to legitimise what Delhi considers Pakistan's illegal occupation of Indian territory is unacceptable and has no bearing on India's sovereignty. 
But Haqqani believes the dispute goes beyond the legalities of borders. 
"The key disagreement between India and China about the border and boundary is geo-strategic, not cartographic," he said. "So there is a limit to what border negotiations and border management mechanisms can achieve." 
Pakistan, he added, remained "China's secondary deterrent against India" - and Beijing's engagement with Islamabad would continue to send that message to Delhi.

articles.title: Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran in UN speech as officials meet on sidelines
articles.summary: In his speech, the US president pondered whether a peace deal would be agreed or whether he would have to take extreme action against Iran.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran if no deal reached By Bernd Debusmann Jr, Khashayar Joneidi, Sarah Smith and Nada Tawfik United Nations General Assembly 
- Published 22 September 2026 
President Donald Trump has told the United Nations General Assembly he faces a "big decision" on whether to strike Iran again or pursue a peace deal. 
A single member of Iran's delegation watched on during the president's speech on Tuesday in New York, in which he said he could "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if the conflict went unresolved. 
Before a standing-room-only audience, Trump also rejected "global government", vowed to broker peace between Russia and Ukraine and ensure the US wins the artificial intelligence race. 
His comments came on a day of high-level diplomacy. He has been meeting more than a dozen world leaders as wars in the Middle East and Ukraine test his foreign policy agenda. 
- 
Live coverage of Trump at UN 
Trump began by touting his accomplishments on the economy, immigration, the border and tackling violent crime, in remarks that sounded more pitched to voters in November's US midterm elections than the diplomats in Manhattan. 
He spent much of his address justifying the war with Iran, which has spiked global oil prices while dragging down his approval ratings since the US and Israel launched the military action in February. 
Trump's tone contrasted with remarks earlier by UN Secretary General António Guterres, who warned global divisions were deepening and underscored the "interdependence" of the world's peoples. 
Image source, EPA Image caption, 
Trump also signed a deal with Denmark to beef up US military presence on Greenland 
The US president argued that the conflict had prevented Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and demonstrated the value of what he described as peace through strength - ultimatums rather than deal-making or compromise. 
"Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?" he said. 
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell?" 
Trump said he believed an Iran deal, which has so far eluded him, would come right after November's elections. 
The remarks were indicative of his foreign-policy strategy of coercive diplomacy - threatening overwhelming force while keeping negotiations open. 
Trump later told reporters that American officials had had a "very productive" three-hour meeting with the Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the general assembly. 
Iran state TV confirmed that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had met US Special Envoy to the Middle East Steve Witkoff, although there was no comment from officials in Tehran. 
The BBC later asked Witkoff how the meeting had gone as he was leaving the UN building and he responded with a thumbs up. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: Moment Trump rebrands Artificial Intelligence to Super Intelligence 
In his speech, Trump once again predicted his diplomacy would end Russia's war in Ukraine, which has shown little sign of letting up as the two sides trade tit-for-tat missile and drone strikes deep into each other's territory. 
"We're working very closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine, and we will get that one done," he said. "It's going to happen, I think, more quickly than people understand." 
Trump also played down fears about AI, vowing that the US would not surrender its lead to China because of alarmism or what he described as a "globalist scheme" to control the technology. 
The US president argued artificial intelligence should instead be known as "super intelligence". 
"The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said. "It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful." 
On the sidelines of the general assembly on Tuesday, Trump signed an agreement with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland to beef up US military presence on the North Atlantic island. 
The deal reaffirms the sovereignty of Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, but grants the US broad access to the island's airspace and territory. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Britain's PM Andy Burnham held his first face-to-face meeting with Trump 
Trump has also been meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and leaders from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman. 
Earlier, Guterres gave his farewell speech as UN secretary general, urging unnamed superpowers to recognise "that their power isn't so super". 
"The fault lines in our world are widening," Guterres said, citing geopolitical rivalries, wars, climate change and artificial intelligence. 
By contrast, Trump criticised international institutions, accusing the UN of a "far-left agenda of globalist bureaucrats who nobody ever elected". 
The US president instead emphasised national sovereignty and "unmatched" American military power. 
"There is no global government," he said. 
He also warned that the US would not allow threats to establish themselves anywhere in the Western hemisphere. 
"If necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States," he said. 
Trump accused Cuba's communist government of cultivating ties to left-wing groups in the US, including the Communist Party USA, Antifa and the Democratic Socialists of America. 
The Cuban delegation also appeared to walk out of the assembly chamber as Trump turned his sights on them, referring to the island as a "failed state".

articles.title: US to build two military bases in Greenland under new deal with Denmark
articles.summary: The defence deal signed at the UN General Assembly also re-affirms Denmark's sovereignty over its semi-autonomous Arctic territory.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
US President Donald Trump signed the deal alongside Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen By Jaroslav Lukiv   and   Adrienne Murray ,  Copenhagen 
- Published 22 September 2026 
The US, Denmark and Greenland have signed a defence deal that allows Washington to build two new military bases in the Arctic territory, while reaffirming Copenhagen's sovereignty over it. 
Before a signing ceremony at the UN General Assembly in New York, US President Donald Trump said "we will immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations". 
Danish PM Mette Frederiksen said the deal was "good for the US, Denmark and Greenland" and also for Europe and Nato, while Greenland's PM Jens-Frederik Nielsen said it was a "win-win-win". 
The three leaders then inked the deal, seemingly ending more than a year of tension over the Arctic territory. 
Trump had threatened to "take" the semi-autonomous Arctic territory over what he said were national security concerns, citing its strategic defence location and its mineral wealth. 
His rhetoric prompted outcry from Greenlanders, Danes and European leaders who issued a joint statement saying his words "undermine transatlantic relations and risk a dangerous downward spiral". 
The deal amends and updates a 1951 defence agreement between Denmark and the US. 
The new pact says the US "shall be allowed to establish an additional Defence Area at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig" - referring to locations in Greenland's south and east. 
Narsarsuaq is a former civilian airport and World War Two base. It has deep-water access and a large runway which US military engineers were recently surveying, the US North Command confirmed to the BBC. 
The Mestersvig outpost is remote, far less developed, and used by a Danish naval dog sled unit. 
The "modalities and technical details" of the bases are yet to be confirmed, and according to the deal, must be mutually agreed by all parties, 
This means the US security arrangements are not unfettered and Greenland and Denmark's approval is still needed. 
Washington currently operates its Pituffik Space Base in Greenland's north-west, and the new deal allows the US to "modernise and expand its activities" there. 
It also says that "no state that is not a member of Nato shall be allowed to establish its own manned or unmanned military installations in Greenland nor shall they be allowed a persistent presence of military forces in Greenland". 
Although the militaries of non-Nato countries are now explicitly barred from the island, it was highly unlikely that non-allied troops would have been allowed access in the first place. 
Critically, no territory is ceded to the US, and it recognises both Denmark's "sovereignty and territorial integrity" and Greenland's right to self-determination. 
On one hand, that's a significant climb down from Trump's earlier calls to acquire the Arctic island. 
But it does deliver a strengthened US military presence and expand on the previous agreement. Therefore to some American eyes, that will be perceived as a historic win. 
The new deal must still be approved by both Denmark's and Greenland's parliaments. 
Despite months of crisis, the mood at Tuesday's signing ceremony appeared strikingly upbeat and friendly. 
"We going to have a tremendous relationship, a secure relationship," Trump said. 
"This is tremendous for Europe and for the United States, for everybody, and for Greenland it's going to be incredible." 
Meanwhile, Frederiksen described the signing of the deal as a "milestone in our long-standing co-operation". 
"Seventy-five years ago we entered into an agreement about the defence of Greenland. Today, we're signing an even bigger and better agreement - a deal that can last forever." 
The Danish prime minister stressed that the agreement "respects sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, as well as Greenland's right to self-determination". 
Jens-Frederik Nielsen said that "for Greenland, it is not only an agreement about us, it is [an] agreement with us. 
"It takes into account the people of Greenland, our rights, our livelihoods and the development of our country. 
"Greenland matters for North American security and for transatlantic security," he said, adding that the Nato had a key role to play in the North Atlantic in a changing security situation. 
The agreement also confirmed Greenland would remain in Nato if it were to gain independence from Denmark. 
The 1951 agreement already allowed the US to send as many troops as it wanted to Greenland. Washington already has more than 100 military personnel permanently stationed at its Pituffik base. 
Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex Greenland, arguing that it was vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China. 
He argued the Arctic island was an essential piece of his plan to build a futuristic "Golden Dome" defence system to protect the US against missile attacks. 
However the deal only mentions the project once, and contains no concrete proposal. 
A Nato spokesperson said shortly afterwards that the military alliance welcomed the deal, which would "help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region". 
In Denmark, the deal is being hailed as a triumph of diplomacy, and several political parties in Denmark have already said they would back it. 
For Greenland, a country of 56,000 people, there was good reason for a big sigh of relief. Its leader sat side-by-side with the world's most powerful man, and got a deal that should now bring an end to months of crisis.

Trump invades the UN with a brutish speech

Gone was any shred of US idealism. It was a spectacle of raw power – a power that is likely to only diminish in the years ahead 
E xpectations were low for Donald Trump’s address to the UN on Tuesday, and yet somehow it was even worse than expected. He does not perform well in formal settings, like chambers of government, preferring a blingier room, like Mar-a-Lago, or an outdoor rally. For years, he has made no secret of his hostility to the UN, and the very principles of international order that define it. 
In recent years, that hostility has deepened into something more like a full-on assault, with frequent attacks on the International Criminal Court (perhaps out of fear that he will someday be indicted), on the UN’s climate agenda, and on Unesco (which the US decided to withdraw from in July 2025). 
His flamboyant effort to launch a so-called Board of Peace in January (just before launching his war of choice on Iran) was another attack on the UN, which, at times, the president wondered if his new creation might simply replace. 
Five months later, it has achieved little in the way of tangible results, except to demand huge sums of money from its small number of member nations, most of which are petrostates. Not one of those states can say that the Middle East is in better shape since the board came into existence, with a crisis that is deepening daily and may engulf Saudi Arabia soon. Trump’s threat to annihilate Iran to UN general assembly is stunning, even for him 
Read more 
But even by Trumpian standards, this was a hollow speech, long on snarling belligerence and short on ideas or policy proposals. The president read robotically from a teleprompter for long stretches, except when he remembered one of the many complaints about the world that he has memorized from his rallies, and a history of grievances that goes back to his rise as a xenophobic developer in the 1980s. 
In short, he insulted nearly everyone in the room, from the Middle Eastern countries who are wondering about the validity of US security guarantees, to the European allies he habitually belittles, to Ukraine, whose leader, Volodymyr Zelensky was in the room, undoubtedly wondering why Trump is now asking him to pause his effective strikes on the Russian invader. 
A famous episode of Seinfeld introduced “Festivus”, a holiday for the sharing of grievances. It felt like that as Trump outlined his Hobbesian vision of the world, with touches of Rodney Dangerfield added in, from a president who complains endlessly that he gets no respect. 
In one stretch, he seemed to be lobbying for a Nobel peace prize while boasting of all the conflicts he has solved, as audience members yawned and checked their phones. He mentioned that these wars had previously been “unendable”, an interesting word that effectively describes two wars today. The Ukraine-Russian war is still going strong despite his frequent promises (including today) to to stop it. 
Then, of course, there is the war of choice in Iran that he launched nearly seven months ago. As he has so many times in his social media outbursts, he ranged erratically from threats to “ annihilate the Islamic Republic ” with car-salesman promises to help Iran achieve greatness if they will just agree do work with him. Which, obviously, they will not, as they continue to defy US threats and even to solidify their position (which has improved markedly with Houthi gains in the last two weeks). 
Trump insisted that stocks of American weapons are increasing, when all news reports are they are rapidly being depleted . 
There was a lengthy assault on climate change, claiming (falsely) that the earth’s climate is cooling, and that the science is a hoax when August tied a record for the hottest month ever recorded, and several important science reports in the last week confirmed how dire the situation is. In Tennessee, the temperature on the field of a football game between the Titans and the Philadelphia Eagles reached 157F. Perhaps that is what the president meant when he bragged that the US is the “hottest” country in the world? He may need a new speechwriter – that claim was also made in his 2025 speech to the UN. 
Another neologism was “super-intelligence”, or “SI”, a term that the president is hoping will suddenly replace “AI”, much as he tried to rename Lake Ontario and the Gulf of Mexico. Time will tell, but it feels unlikely the new term will stick. 
On the eve of an important summit and state dinner with Xi Jinping, this might have been an important moment to stake out ways the US and China might cooperate on AI, to mitigate risks and increase the potential for beneficial research into disease and other problems. That opportunity was not seized. Trump calls on allies to enforce ‘complete economic isolation of Iran’ in UN speech 
Read more 
Other topics that were not addressed included our rapidly deteriorating relationship with Canada , once the US’s greatest ally, and now enraged by Trump’s constant insults. Far from bending Canada to his will, they are achieving the opposite effect, as it always Elbows Up now. It will take years to repair the damage to a vital strategic relationship to the North. 
Instead, more attention was paid to Greenland . The president claimed the US would now be enjoying basing rights – which we already enjoy – and he also suggested that foreign adversaries would not be allowed their bases. That is hardly news – they have never been allowed bases on Greenland. 
While discussing his own vision of sovereignty, including his claims to Venezuelan oil, Trump drew from a sordid page of US history, and quoted a corrupt New York politician, William M “Boss” Tweed, to say “to the victor belong the spoils”. Tweed, the leader of Tammany Hall, was later convicted of stealing tens of millions of dollars from the public, and died in jail. 
Perhaps the saddest aspect of this speech was its utter lack of American idealism – the very force that led to the UN’s creation. In the 250th year of the United States, there were plenty of themes that might have won over a skeptical audience, But there were no inspiring words about fighting poverty, or reducing nuclear tests or keeping weapons out of space (as John F Kennedy promised in 1963). 
Or human rights (introduced as a major theme by Jimmy Carter in 1977), or about reducing tensions with Russia (which Ronald Reagan spoke about in 1988), or the end of the Cold War (which George HW Bush celebrated in 1990), or the need to fight terrorism while avoiding Islamophobia (as Bill Clinton explained carefully in 1998). 
It was just raw power; and a power that is likely to diminish in the years ahead. The power of persuasion has always been critical to presidents coming into the United Nations. But the United States is now at historically low levels of approval around the world, as measured by the Pew Global Attitudes project, with only 23% of people (across 36 nations) expressing confidence in Trump’s leadership. The number is unlikely to go up after today’s performance. 
- 
Ted Widmer, a former White House speechwriter, is the editor of American Speeches, and the recently published The Living Declaration: A Biography of America’s Founding Text, both published by the Library of America
